newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU ministers meet to digest U.S. trade laws.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers meet to digest U.S. trade laws.

text.p: European Union trade ministers will tackle what they consider the unpalatable issue of extra-territorial U.S. trade laws on Wednesday when they sit down for dinner ahead of a policy review meeting.

Anxious to avoid escalating a potentially damaging trade row with Washington, Ireland -- which currently holds the EU presidency -- has asked the 15 ministers to limit the issue to discussion over dinner ahead of Thursday's informal meeting.

The ministers, along with EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan and World Trade Organisation (WTO) chief Renato Ruggiero, are meeting to review the bloc's tactics for the December WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore.

EU diplomats said they would stick to this agenda but would not shirk further criticism of Washington's Helms-Burton Act and D'Amato Bill, which seek to quash investment in Cuba, and Iran and Libya respectively.

Among other things, the Helms-Burton Act allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies which have benefited from investments in property deemed to have been confiscated by Cuba since the communist revolution of 1959.
The D'Amato Bill threatens U.S. government sanctions against foreign companies investing in Iran or Libya's oil industries.

Brittan, given a mandate by EU foreign ministers in July to examine reaction to the laws, will outline possible tit-for-tat counter-proposals. They are due to be agreed by foreign ministers on October 1.
Although the Dublin gathering is informal, Brittan is seeking approval for policies to show EU unity ahead of the Singapore meeting.
Diplomats said the Dublin meeting aims to focus minds on steps needed to extend world trade liberalisation but at the same time protect European industry.
Brittan is under pressure, notably from European parliamentarians, to push developing nations to adhere to Western-style labour standards, including minimum wages and pension guarantees.
But Asian states in particular see this as an attempt to make their industries less competitive and some have vowed to keep the issue off the agenda in Singapore.
Brittan is also expected to brief ministers on proposals for the second phase of liberalising global agreements on textiles and garments.

Last week the European Commission, the EU's executive, warned that its proposals for Singapore were likely to be modest unless major textile and garment exporters came up with better proposals of their own.

Although major textile exporters are not obliged to offer quantitative reductions on their imports, the Commission has warned it would include products on which it had already voluntarily scrapped quotas when accounting for its obligations.

Under a plan to gradually include various textile and garment deals left over from the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade within the WTO, the EU must open its markets next year by a further 17 percent of 1990's import volumes.
